note: Swung more than any other good between dynasties and places, because the state salt monopoly set its price. In days of a laborer's wage, a jin of salt cost 1.2-1.75 under the Song, 0.2 in Wanli Beijing and 0.13 in Beijing in 1736. Where the monopoly was enforced, official salt sold at one and a half to two times the price of private salt (Sichuan 1086: 120 cash against 70-80; the Huai district 1830: 60-70 against 30-odd). Japan's domain salt monopolies are named in the sources, but their effect on price is SILENT.

Swung the most from year to year, but barely drifted. Mitsui's rice moved 15-17% a year and 25-34% over five years. The famines of 1732, 1783-1786 and 1836-1837 doubled or tripled it, and it came back. Kyoto and Osaka rice drifted under 1% a decade before 1859. Across periods it moved with the price level, which about tripled after Japan's 1859 opening.

Firewood was the steadiest good measured: a few percent a year in the Mitsui books, at every gap. Across periods, fuel moved with the price level: Beijing's coal more than doubled in silver from 1615 to 1736.
Steady. Cotton cloth held its price within a period, and Beijing's coarse cloth held from 1615 to 1736 while its flour doubled. Songjiang's cotton cloth swung at the fall of the Ming.

Wages were sticky: Mitsui's Kyoto wage held while prices moved, though a day laborer's pay was flexible. A recoinage raised wages before prices. Rural Beijing's copper wage rose only from 81 to 93 cash a day (1807-1853), while the cash in a tael more than doubled.

Grain and flour moved with the price level across periods: Beijing's flour about doubled in silver from 1615 to 1736, and Song rice quadrupled from before 1068 to 1122. Soybeans swung as much as rice from year to year. For fish, barley, buckwheat, millets and other beans the sources are SILENT.
